query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, dense layer of a noble metal or oxide, such as Si-20Cr-20Fe, on the surface of refractory high-entropy alloys can improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by preventing oxygen penetration and promoting the formation of a protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: depositing a thin, dense layer of a noble metal or oxide
generation.conditions: high-temperature oxidation environment, with temperatures up to 1000 °C
generation.structural_mediator: formation of a protective oxide layer
generation.mechanism: prevention of oxygen penetration and promotion of oxide layer formation
generation.predicted_outcome: improved high-temperature oxygen resistance, with a reduction in weight gain of at least 50% compared to the untreated alloy
generation.uncertainty: the exact composition and thickness of the noble metal or oxide layer may affect the outcome

falsification_experiment.design: exposure of coated and uncoated refractory high-entropy alloys to high-temperature oxidation environment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the weight gain of the coated alloy is not reduced by at least 50% compared to the uncoated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature.
